trivia_fact: Python is named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake. Guido van Rossum was reading Monty Python scripts while developing the language and wanted a short, unique, and slightly mysterious name.

Guido van Rossum started Python as a hobby project during Christmas week 1989. He wanted a successor to the ABC language that would appeal to Unix/C hackers. The first public release (0.9.0) came in February 1991.

Guido van Rossum held the title "Benevolent Dictator for Life" (BDFL) from the late 1990s until he resigned in July 2018 after the contentious PEP 572 (walrus operator) debate. Python is now governed by a five-person Steering Council.

Typing "import this" in a Python interpreter prints 19 aphorisms called The Zen of Python, written by Tim Peters in 1999 (PEP 20). The 20th principle was intentionally left blank: "If you want to add one, propose it."

Python's significant whitespace was a deliberate choice by Guido, inspired by ABC and Donald Knuth's concept of "literate programming." Guido argued that since programmers indent code anyway, the language should enforce it for consistency.

The Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) prevents multiple native threads from executing Python bytecode simultaneously. It was a pragmatic choice in 1992 to simplify memory management. PEP 703 (accepted 2023) began the multi-year project to make the GIL optional.

Python 3.0 was released in December 2008, and Python 2.7 was finally sunset on January 1, 2020 — a 12-year migration period. The transition was so painful it became a cautionary tale in language design about breaking backward compatibility.

Unlike Java or C++ where "this" is implicit, Python requires "self" as the first parameter of instance methods. Guido chose this to make the mechanism transparent and avoid the "magic" of implicit variables. Multiple PEPs to change this were rejected.

Python's list comprehensions were borrowed from Haskell and added in Python 2.0 (2000). The syntax [x for x in items] mirrors mathematical set-builder notation. Dictionary and set comprehensions followed in Python 2.7/3.0.

Python's "batteries included" philosophy means the standard library ships with modules for nearly everything — email, HTTP, JSON, SQLite, XML, compression, and more. The phrase was coined in the late 1990s to describe this intentional richness.

PEP 572 introduced the walrus operator (:=) for assignment expressions in Python 3.8. The debate was so heated that it directly led to Guido van Rossum's resignation as BDFL. The operator is called "walrus" because := looks like walrus eyes and tusks.

Python's documentation uses "spam," "eggs," and "ham" as metasyntactic variables instead of the traditional "foo" and "bar." This is a direct homage to the Monty Python "Spam" sketch, reinforcing the language's comedic heritage.

The reference implementation is called CPython because it's written in C. Other implementations include Jython (Java), IronPython (.NET), PyPy (Python in Python with JIT), and MicroPython (microcontrollers). When people say "Python," they almost always mean CPython.

Python Enhancement Proposals (PEPs) are the formal mechanism for proposing changes to Python. PEP 1 defines the process itself. There are over 700 PEPs, and the most famous rejected one is PEP 3003 — the language moratorium that froze syntax changes for Python 3.1-3.2.

Python was a niche scripting language for most of its first 15 years. Its rise to the #1 TIOBE index position in October 2021 was driven largely by data science, machine learning, and beginner-friendly coding education — none of which Guido originally designed it for.
